headline: A trade deal, then Wuhan is locked down
text: On 15 January the US and China signed a 'phase one' trade deal: China will buy $200 billion more of US goods and services over two years. On 23 January China sealed off the city of Wuhan to stop a new coronavirus, and lockdowns spread to other cities.
imageCaption: Signing of the phase-one trade deal, White House, 15 January 2020

headline: Soleimani killed, then Iran shoots down a Ukrainian airliner
text: A US drone strike killed General Qasem Soleimani, head of the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, at Baghdad airport on 3 January. Iran fired missiles at US bases in Iraq on 8 January; hours later the Revolutionary Guards shot down Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752 after take-off from Tehran, killing all 176 aboard, among them 82 Iranians and 63 Canadians, many of them Iranian-Canadian students and academics. After three days of denial, Iran admitted on 11 January that it had downed the plane by mistake, and protesters took to the streets.
imageCaption: Crowds fill Azadi Square in Tehran for the funeral procession of Qasem Soleimani, 6 January 2020

headline: Shanghai and profits send Tesla soaring
text: Tesla said on 29 January that 2019 was a turning point: it returned to profit in the second half and generated 1.1 billion dollars of free cash flow. Its Shanghai factory, its first outside the US, started building the Model 3 less than ten months after construction began, and production of the Model Y has started in Fremont. The shares rose more than 50% in January.
source: Tesla Q4 and FY2019 Update, 29 January 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1318605/000156459020002489/tsla-ex991_340.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla,_Inc. (Gigafactory Shanghai, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Aerial view of the Tesla Gigafactory in Shanghai

headline: The coronavirus reaches the markets: the fastest fall from a record
text: The S&P 500 closed at a record 3,386.15 on 19 February. Then the new coronavirus spread beyond China, and in the week of 24 to 28 February markets had their largest weekly falls since the 2008 crisis, the fastest slide from a record ever seen. The S&P 500 ended February down 8% at 2,954.22. The virus reached northern Italy, where towns were sealed off, and Switzerland, which confirmed its first case on 25 February and on 28 February banned events with more than 1,000 people. Oil fell with shares: US crude closed February at about 45 dollars, from 61 at the end of December, and ExxonMobil lost 17%.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closing_milestones_of_the_S%26P_500 (read 2026-10-03); data/reference/sp500.json; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Switzerland (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 31 January 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408820000011/f8k4q991.htm (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: A screen is reflected in a trader's eyes at the opening bell of the New York Stock Exchange as the coronavirus sell-off deepens, 27 February 2020
imageCredit: Photo by JOHANNES EISELE/AFP via Getty Images

headline: Thiam resigns over the spying affair
text: In the final months of 2019 it emerged that Credit Suisse had had former executives, among them the wealth manager Iqbal Khan, followed by private detectives; the chief operating officer Pierre-Olivier Bouée left. On 7 February Tidjane Thiam announced his resignation as chief executive. Thomas Gottstein, head of the Swiss bank, succeeds him on 14 February. At the end of the month markets began to fall as the coronavirus spread.
imageCaption: Tidjane Thiam presents his last annual results as chief executive of Credit Suisse, Zurich, February 2020

headline: Saudi-Russian price war as the world locks down
text: Russia rejected OPEC's call for deeper cuts on 6 March. Saudi Arabia answered by cutting its prices and announcing it would raise output from 9.7 to 12.3 million barrels a day. On 9 March oil fell about a quarter and stock markets crashed. As lockdowns spread, US crude fell to $20.48 on 18 March and ended the month down 54%. Schlumberger lost half its value in March and ExxonMobil 26 percent.
imageCaption: Russian energy minister Alexander Novak arrives at the OPEC meeting in Vienna at which Russia refused deeper cuts, 6 March 2020
imageCredit: Photo by ALEX HALADA/AFP via Getty Images

headline: Pandemic: the world shuts down
text: The WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March. Italy locked down on 9 March, the United States barred travellers from Europe, and on 16 March the Swiss government declared an 'extraordinary situation', closing schools, shops, restaurants and borders; on 20 March it announced a 42 billion franc aid package. Stock markets crashed: the Dow lost 7.8 percent on 9 March, 10 percent on 12 March and 12.9 percent on 16 March, when trading was halted by circuit breakers for the third time that month and the VIX fear index closed at a record 82.69. The Fed cut rates to zero, and Congress passed a 2.2 trillion dollar relief law on 27 March; the S&P 500, 34 percent below its February record on 23 March, ended the month down 13 percent. Daimler (down 27 percent) and BMW (down 20 percent) shut their car factories, Glencore fell 38 percent, Citigroup 34 percent and General Electric 27 percent, while McDonald's served only through drive-thrus and Coca-Cola, which sells much of its drinks in restaurants and stadiums, lost 17 percent.

headline: Back to zero, and unlimited bond buying
text: As the coronavirus spread, the Fed cut its rate by half a point on 3 March and, on Sunday 15 March, to 0 to 0.25 percent, with at least 500 billion dollars of Treasury and 200 billion of mortgage-bond purchases. On 23 March it promised to buy bonds 'in the amounts needed' and, for the first time, to buy corporate bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield averaged 0.9 percent in March, a record low.
imageCaption: Fed Chair Jerome Powell announces an emergency half-point rate cut, Washington, 3 March 2020

headline: Pandemic on top of the MAX: Boeing suspends its dividend
text: With air travel collapsing because of Covid-19 and the MAX still grounded, Boeing on 20 March suspended its dividend and extended its halt on buybacks; chief executive Dave Calhoun gives up his pay for the year. On 23 March it said it will stop production in the Seattle area for 14 days.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/12927/000001292720000030/exhibit991.htm (Boeing release of 2020-03-20, read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/12927/000001292720000033/exhibit991.htm (Boeing release of 2020-03-23, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Lufthansa's grounded fleet parked on a runway at Frankfurt airport, 27 March 2020

headline: Iger hands over to Chapek; then the pandemic closes the parks
text: On 25 February Bob Iger stepped down as chief executive and was succeeded by Bob Chapek, head of the parks division; Iger stays as executive chairman. In mid-March, as the coronavirus spread, Disney closed Disneyland, Walt Disney World and Disneyland Paris and suspended its cruises; its parks in Asia were already shut. Cinemas closed too.
imageCaption: Magic Kingdom at Walt Disney World stands empty, closed to the public because of the coronavirus, Orlando, 23 March 2020

headline: Pekka Lundmark to replace Rajeev Suri
text: On 2 March Nokia named Pekka Lundmark, chief executive of the Finnish energy company Fortum, as its next chief executive, as it struggles to keep pace with Huawei and Ericsson in 5G contracts. Markets then fell sharply with the spread of the coronavirus.

headline: Oil goes negative
text: OPEC, Russia and others agreed on 9 to 12 April to cut output by 9.7 million barrels a day, about 10% of world supply. It was not enough: on 20 April the expiring May contract for US crude fell to minus $37 a barrel, as storage at Cushing, Oklahoma filled up and holders paid to get rid of oil. Brent fell to about $9 the next day. ExxonMobil had cut its 2020 capital spending by 30 percent, to about 23 billion dollars, on 7 April; its shares rose 22% as stocks rebounded.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Russia%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_oil_price_war (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OPEC (read 2026-10-03); https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET&s=RWTC&f=D (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 7 April 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408820000028/f8k1q991.htm (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Crude oil storage tanks at Cushing, Oklahoma, the delivery point for US crude, in the week the price went below zero, 23 April 2020

headline: The best month since 1987, in the middle of a pandemic
text: With the Fed's emergency lending programmes and the 2 trillion dollar CARES Act behind them, shares more than won back their late-March losses, led by energy, consumer and health-care companies. The S&P 500 rose 13% in April to 2,912.43, its best month since January 1987, though still well below February's record and with unemployment soaring.
imageCaption: The New York Stock Exchange, whose trading floor is closed for the first time in its history because of the coronavirus, 19 April 2020

headline: Profitable even in a pandemic quarter
text: On 29 April Tesla reported a profit for the first quarter, the first time it has been profitable in the seasonally weak first quarter, despite factory closures. It was its third profitable quarter in a row.
imageCaption: A Tesla Model 3, Xiamen, China

headline: Locked-down shoppers turn to eBay
text: On April 29 eBay reported first-quarter revenue of $2.4 billion, 174 million active buyers and gave a business update on Covid-19, which is sending shoppers online. Jamie Iannone has just become chief executive.
imageCaption: eBay's campus in Willow Glen, San Jose

headline: The pandemic sends shoppers to Amazon
text: With shops closed by the Covid-19 pandemic, Amazon is hiring about 175,000 extra warehouse and delivery workers. On April 30 it reported first-quarter sales of $75.5 billion, up 26%; net income fell to $2.5 billion from $3.6 billion.
imageCaption: Amazon Prime delivery vans

headline: Schlumberger cuts its dividend by 75 percent
text: On 9 April Saudi Arabia and Russia agreed to cut output by about 10 million barrels a day; on 20 April US crude briefly fell to minus 37 dollars. On 17 April Schlumberger cut its quarterly dividend by 75 percent to 12.5 cents and took an 8.5 billion dollar charge, mostly writing down goodwill after the collapse in market values in March. Stock markets rebounded strongly from their lows.
imageCaption: An oil pumpjack in the Permian Basin, Texas

headline: Sony to become Sony Group and buy out its finance arm
text: On 19 May Sony said it will rename itself Sony Group Corporation from April 2021, with the electronics business taking the Sony Corporation name, and will make Sony Financial Holdings, of which it owns about 65%, a wholly owned subsidiary through a takeover bid.
imageCaption: The Sony Building in the Ginza district, Tokyo

headline: Pandemic shoppers stock up at Walmart
text: Walmart reported that in the three months to April net sales rose 11% and online sales 74%, as Americans stocked up during the coronavirus lockdowns. Customers came less often but bought 16.5% more per visit, and profit rose 4% despite higher costs.
imageCaption: Pandemic shopping rules at a Walmart store, New York, 2020 ;;

headline: Stuck at home, the world goes online: Nasdaq above 10,000
text: The Nasdaq closed above 10,000 for the first time on 10 June, less than three months after falling to 6,861 on 23 March in the pandemic crash. With offices, shops and schools closed, people work, shop and learn online, and the largest technology companies have gained most.
imageCaption: The Nasdaq MarketSite tower in Times Square, New York

headline: Test flights for the MAX's return
text: From 28 June the FAA began three days of certification flight tests of the modified 737 MAX, a key step toward letting it fly again. Stock markets have recovered much of their spring losses as economies reopen.
imageCaption: Boeing 737 MAX, 2023

headline: Masks on trains and buses
text: From July masks became mandatory on public transport in Switzerland. Shops and schools reopened in May, and most of the spring measures have been lifted step by step, but the virus has not gone away.

headline: Tesla becomes the world's most valuable car maker
text: In July Tesla became the world's most valuable car maker by stock-market value, although it builds far fewer cars than the big established makers. It also reported a fourth straight quarterly profit, which meets a condition for joining the S&P 500 index.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla,_Inc. ('Starting in July 2020, it has been the world's most valuable automaker', read 2026-10-03); CNBC, 'Tesla stock jumps on carmaker's addition to the S&P 500', 16 November 2020, https://www.cnbc.com/2020/11/16/tesla-stock-jumps-on-news-company-is-joining-sp-500.html (profit record, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Tesla Model Y, 2026

headline: Intel's 7-nanometre chips slip, and it may outsource
text: On 23 July Intel said its first 7-nanometre chips are six months later than planned, now due in late 2022 or early 2023, with production yields about a year behind target. Chief executive Bob Swan said Intel might have other companies make some chips. The shares fell 16% the next day.
source: https://www.cnn.com/2020/07/24/investing/intel-earnings-stock-selloff (read 2026-10-03, via search summary); https://siliconangle.com/2020/07/23/intels-stock-falls-delays-first-7nm-computer-chips/ (read 2026-10-03, via search summary)
imageCaption: Intel's D1X chip development factory under construction, Hillsboro, Oregon

headline: eBay sells its classifieds business
text: eBay agreed to sell its classified-ads business, including Germany's Kleinanzeigen, to Adevinta for $2.5 billion in cash and 540 million Adevinta shares.

headline: Back at a record, five months after the crash
text: On 18 August the S&P 500 closed above its February record, less than five months after the March low. The S&P 500 rose 7% in August to 3,500.31, while the pandemic still kept much of the economy closed.
imageCaption: People walk past the Fearless Girl statue and the New York Stock Exchange as the city reopens, 3 August 2020

headline: Gold at a record as the Fed says it will let inflation run
text: Gold averaged 1,969 dollars in August, beating its 2011 record. With the Fed's rate at zero, the 10-year Treasury yield averaged only 0.65 percent, below inflation of about 1 percent (July). On 27 August the Fed said it would now aim for inflation that 'averages 2 percent over time', allowing it to run 'moderately above 2 percent for some time' after periods below.
imageCaption: The gold vault of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York

headline: Buffett buys into Japan's trading houses
text: Berkshire Hathaway said it has bought just over 5% of each of Japan's five biggest trading houses, Itochu, Marubeni, Mitsubishi, Mitsui and Sumitomo, over the past year, worth over $6 billion.

headline: Tesla splits its shares five for one
text: On 11 August Tesla announced a five-for-one stock split, to make the shares more accessible to employees and investors; shareholders on record on 21 August receive four extra shares for each one. The shares rose 74% in August.
source: Tesla 8-K exhibit 'Tesla Announces a Five-for-One Stock Split', 11 August 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1318605/000156459020039353/tsla-ex991_6.htm (read 2026-10-03); data/out/tsla.json (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: The Nasdaq trading studio in Times Square, New York, where Tesla shares trade

headline: Two trillion dollars
text: On 19 August Apple's shares briefly topped 467 dollars, making it the first US company worth two trillion dollars, despite the pandemic. Apple has also announced that it will move its Macs from Intel processors to chips of its own design.
imageCaption: Apple Park, Cupertino

headline: Covid-19 cuts Cisco's sales
text: Cisco reported fiscal-year revenue of $49.3 billion, down 5%, with fourth-quarter revenue down 9%, and forecast a decline of 9% to 11% for the next quarter. It has completed the acquisition of ThousandEyes, which monitors internet and cloud performance.

headline: Berkshire buys into Japan's five big trading houses
text: On 31 August Berkshire said it had bought slightly more than 5% of each of Japan's five leading trading companies, Itochu, Marubeni, Mitsubishi, Mitsui and Sumitomo, over about twelve months. It intends to hold them for the long term and may go up to 9.9% in each.

headline: No dividend this year
text: On 6 August Glencore said it would pay no distribution to shareholders in 2020 so as to cut its $19.7bn net debt. It reported a first-half net loss of $2.6bn after $3.2bn of write-downs, while its trading arm made a record $2.0bn of adjusted EBIT.

headline: An exclusive licence to OpenAI's GPT-3
text: On 22 September Microsoft announced an exclusive licence to use GPT-3, the language-generating artificial intelligence model of OpenAI, in which it invested in 2019. The same week it agreed to buy ZeniMax Media, owner of Bethesda Softworks, for about 7.5 billion dollars.

headline: Nvidia agrees to buy Arm for 40 billion dollars
text: On 13 September Nvidia agreed to buy Arm, the British designer of the processors in almost all smartphones, from SoftBank for 40 billion dollars, subject to approval by regulators; SoftBank would keep about 10% of Nvidia.
imageCaption: Arm's headquarters in Cambridge, England

headline: Siemens Energy is spun off
text: Shares of Siemens Energy, the former gas and power division, began trading in Frankfurt on 28 September after Siemens shareholders approved the split in July. Siemens shareholders received Siemens Energy shares; Siemens keeps a minority stake.
imageCaption: Siemens' gas turbine plant on Huttenstrasse, Berlin-Moabit

headline: Regulators order Citigroup to fix 'longstanding deficiencies'
text: The Federal Reserve ordered Citigroup on 7 October to correct longstanding deficiencies in its risk management, data quality and internal controls, and its bank regulator fined it $400 million. In August Citibank had mistakenly wired $900 million to lenders of the cosmetics company Revlon. Jane Fraser, named in September, will succeed Michael Corbat as chief executive in February 2021, the first woman to lead one of the four biggest U.S. banks.
imageCaption: 388 Greenwich Street, Citigroup's headquarters in Lower Manhattan

headline: IBM to split off its old infrastructure services
text: On 8 October IBM announced it will spin off its managed infrastructure services unit into a separate listed company, keeping hybrid cloud and artificial intelligence. The unit runs IT for about 4,600 clients in 115 countries with a 60 billion dollar backlog. Chief executive Arvind Krishna, formerly head of IBM's cloud business and research, took over from Ginni Rometty in April and credits the Red Hat purchase with making the split possible.
imageCaption: Arvind Krishna, IBM's chief executive

headline: Nokia to build a mobile network on the Moon
text: In October NASA chose Nokia, through Bell Labs, to build a 4G mobile network for astronauts on the Moon, a 14.1 million dollar contract. In June Nokia won a 5G contract worth about 450 million dollars as sole supplier to Taiwan Mobile.

headline: Biden wins, and a vaccine works
text: Joe Biden won the US election of 3 November, with 306 electoral votes and about 51 percent of the vote, and was declared the winner by the media on 7 November; President Trump refuses to concede and claims fraud without evidence. On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech announced that their vaccine was about 90 percent effective in trials. Investors rushed into the shares hurt most by the pandemic: Schlumberger and Glencore rose about 40%, General Electric 37%, Citigroup 33%, Daimler 30%, BMW 28% and UBS 22%, and US crude rose 27% to $45.20. The Dow closed above 30,000 for the first time on 24 November, and the S&P 500 rose 11% in the month.

imageCaption: Crowds celebrate Joe Biden's election victory, Washington, 7 November 2020

headline: A vaccine, and the MAX is cleared to fly
text: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech said their Covid-19 vaccine was more than 90% effective, and travel stocks soared. On 18 November the FAA ended the 737 MAX's 20-month grounding, the longest ever for a US airliner, subject to fixes on each plane and new pilot training.
imageCaption: A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 MAX 8 at the gate

headline: Tesla will join the S&P 500
text: S&P Dow Jones Indices announced on 16 November that Tesla will join the S&P 500 index on 21 December, after five consecutive quarterly profits. Index funds will have to buy the shares; Tesla will be one of the ten most valuable companies in the index. The shares jumped more than 13% in after-hours trading.
source: CNBC, 'Tesla stock jumps on carmaker's addition to the S&P 500', 16 November 2020, https://www.cnbc.com/2020/11/16/tesla-stock-jumps-on-news-company-is-joining-sp-500.html (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla,_Inc. (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: The New York Stock Exchange, Wall Street

headline: Disney+ passes 73 million subscribers in its first year
text: On 12 November Disney reported a loss for its business year because of the pandemic, but said Disney+ had more than 73 million paying subscribers after one year, 'far surpassing our expectations'.
imageCaption: Disney+

headline: A vaccine lifts oil shares; ExxonMobil writes off up to 20 billion
text: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech said their Covid vaccine was more than 90 percent effective in its first analysis, and oil shares, among the hardest hit by the pandemic, jumped. US crude rose from about 36 to 45 dollars during the month. On 30 November ExxonMobil said it would take a 17 to 20 billion dollar write-down on gas fields it no longer plans to develop, cut spending further and reduce its workforce by 15 percent by the end of 2021, while keeping the dividend.
source: Pfizer and BioNTech press release of 9 November 2020 (BioNTech Form 6-K exhibit 99.1), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1776985/000156459020052228/ (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 30 November 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408820000093/xomexhibit9911302020.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Darren Woods, chairman and chief executive of ExxonMobil

headline: 'Accelerating the Arches': digital, delivery and drive-thru
text: On 9 November chief executive Chris Kempczinski announced a new growth strategy, 'Accelerating the Arches', focused on marketing, core menu items (burgers, chicken and coffee) and the 'three Ds': digital, delivery and drive-thru, which proved their worth during the pandemic.
imageCaption: A McDonald's delivery bicycle ;;

headline: The first vaccinations
text: On 23 December Switzerland began vaccinating against COVID-19, four days after the regulator Swissmedic approved the first vaccine. Restaurants, sports and cultural venues have been closed again since the cases rose in the autumn.

headline: 2020 in review: crash and recovery, up 16 percent
text: The S&P 500 ended 2020 at 3,756.07, up 16%, after falling 34% between February and March; the Dow gained 7.3%. Interest rates near zero, huge government spending and the vaccines carried shares to records despite the pandemic.

headline: Disney+ reaches 86.8 million; Disney raises its streaming targets
text: At an investor day on 10 December Disney said Disney+ had 86.8 million subscribers, a year after launch, and laid out plans for dozens of new Marvel and Star Wars series and films for streaming.
imageCaption: Disney+

headline: Glasenberg to retire; Nagle, the coal boss, to succeed
text: On 4 December Glencore said Ivan Glasenberg, chief executive since 2002, will step down in the first half of 2021, to be succeeded by Gary Nagle, 45, who runs its coal business from Sydney. The same day it set a target to cut its total emissions 40% by 2035 from 2019 levels and an ambition of net zero by 2050, by running down its coal mines rather than selling them. China has stopped buying Australian coal.
imageCaption: Ivan Glasenberg, Glencore's chief executive for eighteen years, at a press conference
